sections.history: Thiruvellarai, about 22 km from Tiruchirappalli on the Thuraiyur road, is one of the 108 Divya Desams in Chola Nadu, sung by Periyalvar and Thirumangai Alvar in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham. Periyalvar devotes a full decad of the Periyalvar Tirumozhi to this Lord. Two rock-cut caves here carry three inscriptions: two of the Pallava king Nandivarman II and one of Dantivarman, placing the shrine firmly in the eighth and ninth centuries. The swastika-shaped tank outside the complex is recorded as the work of Kamban Araiyan, about 800 CE, in Dantivarman's reign. The medieval Cholas, later Pandyas, Vijayanagara rulers and Madurai Nayaks added to the temple in turn.
sections.architecture: The temple stands on an artificial rise of white rock, some fifteen metres high, from which the name Thiruvellarai — the white rock — is understood. Pundarikakshan stands facing east beneath the Vimalakruthi Vimanam, with Pankajavalli in her own shrine. The sanctum has two stepped entrances, the Uttarayana Vasal and the Dakshinayana Vasal, opened according to the sun's course. Pallava sculptures of Narasimha and Varaha survive, as do Vijayanagara and Nayak wall paintings in the main shrine. The rajagopuram was never completed.
sections.legends: Tradition credits the founding of the shrine to the king Sibi Chakravarti, and local belief holds it to be very ancient. The Lord is called Pundarikakshan, the lotus-eyed, and is known locally as Mayavan during the southward half of the sun's year and as Thai Matha Nayagan in the northward half. The two sanctum doors recall this turning of the year: devotees enter by the Dakshinayana door in the one season and the Uttarayana door in the other, as the pilgrimage of the sun is itself honoured.
sections.festivals: The Vaishnava year is kept here, with Vaikunta Ekadashi among its great days. The opening and shifting of the two sanctum entrances at the sun's turning, around Thai and again in the Tamil months of Aadi to Margazhi, is a distinctive observance of this temple. Confirm festival dates locally, as they follow the Tamil almanac.
sections.experience: The climb up the stone steps to the lotus-eyed Lord is part of the devotion. Walk slowly past the Pallava carvings and the faded paintings, notice the double sanctum entrance, and look down on the swastika-shaped tank. The temple is quiet, and a good half-day pilgrimage from Tiruchirappalli.

visit.timings: Open daily with morning and evening darshan sessions and a midday closure; Vaikunta Ekadashi is the busiest day. Confirm current timings before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Thiruvellarai is about 22 km from Tiruchirappalli, past Mannachanallur on the Thuraiyur road. Tiruchirappalli Junction and Tiruchirappalli International Airport are the nearest rail and air gateways; buses and taxis cover the road journey.
